passage:
Monday. Ujjwal, five, watered the class plants and shared his crayons. Parveen ma'am said, "Good job, Ujjwal!" three times.
Tuesday. He spilled paint on Mehul's drawing, and Parveen ma'am said sharply, "Ujjwal, look where you're going!" He stood very still, lip wobbling.
Friday. At home, Papa asked, "How was school this week?" Ujjwal hugged his knees. "Parveen ma'am shouted at me." He didn't mention the plants, or the crayons, or the three "good jobs". Papa asked, "Anything nice?" Ujjwal thought hard, then shrugged.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday?
qa.a: He spilled paint on Mehul's drawing.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal only talk about being shouted at?
qa.a: The sharp moment hurt and stuck with him, so it felt bigger than the three 'good jobs' from Monday.

qa.q: How could Papa help Ujjwal remember the good parts of his week?
qa.a: Papa could gently ask about the class plants or sharing crayons, and tell him that one spill doesn't undo all the good things he did.

qa.q: How might Parveen ma'am feel if she heard Ujjwal's version of the week?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little sad that one sharp moment counted more for him than her praise, and might soften her tone next time.

grounding: It shows a young boy remembering one scolding far more than several moments of praise.

passage:
The power had gone out in the Kolkata flat, and Arnab, four, couldn't sleep in the heat. His mother Gopika fanned him with a newspaper. "What was the best part of today?"
Arnab's lip trembled. "Dadu said I was naughty."
He had pulled the cat's tail once, in the morning. After that he'd sung for Dadu, fed the fish and eaten all his rice, and Dadu had clapped each time.
"Dadu also clapped when you sang," Gopika said softly.
"But he said naughty." Arnab turned his face to the wall.
Gopika kept fanning, and began to hum his song.

qa.q: What did Arnab do after pulling the cat's tail?
qa.a: He sang for Dadu, fed the fish and ate all his rice.

qa.q: Why does 'naughty' matter more to Arnab than all the clapping?
qa.a: The one scolding hurt, so it feels heavier and stays in his mind, pushing out the happy moments.

qa.q: What else could Gopika try to help Arnab?
qa.a: She could name each good moment with him slowly, like the song and the fish, or ask Dadu to remind him tomorrow how much he enjoyed the singing. 🙂

qa.q: How might Dadu feel if he knew Arnab went to bed upset?
qa.a: Dadu might feel sorry that one word stuck, when he clapped far more than he scolded.

grounding: It shows a small boy on a hot, dark night holding on to one scolding more than many moments of praise.

passage:
At Tenzin's school in Bengaluru, Nirmala miss put stickers on the chart every day. Tenzin, six, had five gold stars for reading and one frowning face from the day he pushed in the lunch line.
At pick-up his uncle said, "Show me your chart!"
Tenzin pointed straight at the frowning face. "That's me. I was bad."
"And these?" His uncle tapped the stars.
"Those are just stars." Tenzin kicked a pebble. "Nirmala miss was cross."
His uncle crouched down. "Five stars and one frown. Which is more?" Tenzin counted on his fingers, frowning.

qa.q: How many gold stars did Tenzin have?
qa.a: Five gold stars for reading.

qa.q: What does Tenzin pointing straight at the frowning face suggest?
qa.a: That the one telling-off hurt and felt like the truth about him, so it outweighed the five stars he'd earned.

qa.q: What is good about the uncle's question?
qa.a: Asking him to count stars and frowns lets Tenzin see for himself that the good outnumbers the bad, without being told to cheer up.

qa.q: How might Nirmala miss feel if she saw Tenzin calling himself bad?
qa.a: She might be surprised that one frowning face mattered more than the stars, and want to tell him he's a good reader who made one mistake.

grounding: It shows a young boy fixing on one frowning sticker over five gold stars.

passage:
"Ma, Mamu shouted at me."
"When, Arnab?"
"At the wedding. I touched the flowers on the car."
Gopika looked at him in the rear-view mirror. "And what about when you danced? Everyone clapped. Nani said you were the best dancer."
"Mamu shouted."
"And the aunty who gave you two laddoos for helping carry the plates?"
Arnab pulled his knees up. "He said DON'T in a big voice."
"Mamu said sorry after, remember? He lifted you up."
"But he shouted first." Arnab looked out of the window, his lip wobbling.

qa.q: What did Arnab touch at the wedding?
qa.a: He touched the flowers on the car.

qa.q: Why does Arnab keep coming back to Mamu shouting?
qa.a: The one loud "DON'T" hurt and scared him, so it feels much bigger than the clapping, the laddoos and even Mamu's sorry 🥺

qa.q: What could Gopika try next to help Arnab with the hurt?
qa.a: She could first say that the shout felt scary, and then, once he feels heard, remind him of the dancing and the clapping.

qa.q: How might Mamu feel if he heard that the shout was all Arnab remembered?
qa.a: Mamu might feel sorry and surprised, since he apologised and lifted Arnab up, and never meant one sharp word to spoil the day.

grounding: It shows a young child remembering one scolding more strongly than many moments of praise at a family wedding.

passage:
Dance teacher's note, Saturday kids' class (Harsha)
Uday, 5, had a lovely class. I praised him five times: his jumps, helping a new girl, the clap pattern, waiting his turn, his big smile.
Once he pushed past another child, and I said firmly, "Uday, no pushing."
At pick-up he told his father, "Harsha teacher doesn't like me. She said no pushing." Nothing else.
I knelt and told him I liked his jumps and his helping, and that "no pushing" was about the pushing, not about him. He still looked unsure.
Next: repeat the praise at the start of next class; keep reminders short.

qa.q: How many times did Harsha praise Uday?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he said Harsha teacher doesn't like him?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unsure, because the one firm "no pushing" felt heavier than all five bits of praise.

qa.q: Which step by Harsha could help Uday most, and why?
qa.a: Kneeling down to separate the pushing from Uday himself, and planning to repeat the praise next class, helps the good moments stick as firmly as the one telling-off.

qa.q: How might Uday's father see the class after hearing "Harsha teacher doesn't like me"?
qa.a: His father might worry at first that Uday had a bad day, until he learns from Harsha about the five kind comments.

grounding: It shows a young child remembering one firm correction far more strongly than several moments of praise.
